Juvenile and adult Cape elephantfish (Callorhinchus capensis) exhibit notable differences in their body size and life-history parameters. The fork length at birth has been estimated at approximately 10.6 cm [Lb = approximately 10.6 cm], a modest size that reflects the constraints of egg case development and the limited space within the capsule. Upon reaching sexual maturity, individuals ultimately attain a maximum fork length of approximately 98 cm [Li = approximately 98 cm], though total length measurements provided by the IUCN suggest some adults may reach up to 120 cm total length. These fork length values are consistent with those reported for other members of the genus Callorhinchus. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is approximately 5000 grams [Wwi = approximately 5000 grams], placing this species among the larger elephantfishes within its family. This substantial body mass supports a relatively extended lifespan and a slow pace of life, as is typical for many chimaeroid fishes.

Reproductive biology in this species is characterized by a slow life history. Under thermal conditions typical of its temperate habitat, approximately 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is achieved through the production of two egg cases per year [Ri = two egg cases per year]. This modest annual fecundity is a common trait among holocephalans and stands in contrast to the far higher fecundities observed in many elasmobranchs. The extended incubation period associated with this thermal regime, together with the relatively small brood size, suggests a reproductive strategy oriented toward high offspring survival rather than high fecundity. Females invest considerable resources into each egg capsule, which provides a protective structure and a substantial yolk reserve for the developing embryo. This allocation strategy is reflected in the slow population turnover typical of the species.

Female Cape elephantfish reach sexual maturity at a fork length of approximately 49.6 cm [Lp = approximately 49.6 cm], a size that is reached after a prolonged juvenile phase. At a water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the age at first reproduction for females is approximately 1533 days after birth [tR = approximately 1533 days after birth], a value that aligns with the slow maturation typical of chimaeroids. Males, in contrast, mature somewhat earlier, reaching first reproduction at approximately 1204 days after birth [tR = approximately 1204 days after birth] at this temperature. This difference in maturation timing between the sexes is a common pattern in many chondrichthyans and is thought to reflect differing selective pressures on males and females. The onset of reproductive activity is a critical milestone in the life cycle, representing the transition from an immature, somatic-growth-oriented phase to a reproductively active adult stage that allocates energy toward egg case production and mating.

The embryonic development of this species takes place within a tough, horny egg capsule. At the typical temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the age at birth is approximately 275 days [ab = approximately 275 days], a gestation period that corresponds well with the IUCN estimate of nine to twelve months. This extended developmental duration is a consequence of the cool thermal environment and the large amount of yolk that must be metabolized before hatching. Upon emergence, the neonate is fully formed and already measures around 10.6 cm [Lb = around 10.6 cm], a relatively large size at birth that reduces vulnerability to predation during the early juvenile period. The extended incubation period also ensures that young are born at a time of year when prey availability is high, improving their chances of survival during the vulnerable exotrophic transition.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Cape elephantfish under natural conditions at 12 °C [T = 12 °C] is approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years], a longevity that is moderate among chimaeroids but still places the species on the slow end of the life-history continuum. This extended lifespan, combined with late maturation and low fecundity, renders the species particularly susceptible to overexploitation. The slow pace of life is also reflected in the growth rate; individuals spend several years as juveniles before reaching the size at which gonad maturation and first reproduction become possible. The ultimate fork length of 98 cm [Li = 98 cm] is typically reached only after many years of sustained growth, and adults may continue to grow slowly throughout their reproductive lives.
